video_title: Ukraine War: Putin, Zelenskyy, Trump, Drones and the Future of Warfare | Lex Fridman Podcast #504
transcript: - The following is a conversation with Preston Stewart and Michael Kofman about the war in Ukraine. Preston is a West Point graduate and Afghanistan veteran who covers the war extensively on his YouTube channel called Preston Stewart, his podcast called War and Conflict, and his newsletter called Defense Tech News. Michael is a world-class military analysis expert specializing in the Russian and Ukrainian militaries. He is a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment, and he hosts the Russia Contingency Podcast on the War on the Rocks platform. Please follow and support their work. This is the Lex Fridman Podcast. To support it, please check out our sponsors in the description, where you can also find links to contact me, ask questions, give feedback, and so on. And now, dear friends, here's Preston Stewart and Michael Kofman. Gentlemen, thank you for doing this late-night conversation. Let's see how long we go. The war in Ukraine is in its fifth year. Let's lay out what is the state of the war in terms of territories, in terms of battles, in terms of everything that you talk about from a military perspective. Mike, do you want to go first? - Yeah, sure. I think that the war had probably an inflection point last year, and most people recognize that this year for Ukraine is the best year of combat performance for them on the ground since probably about the summer of twenty twenty-three offensive. But there's a dichotomy to it because on the one hand, Ukraine's doing really well along the front line, but it faces the challenge of an expansive Russian strike campaign and the cumulative damage that has been inflicted to Ukrainian infrastructure, both energy and all sorts of civilian types of infrastructure over the course of several years. And so the winter is quite uncertain on what's going to happen in Ukraine's population centers. Now, I know Ukraine has proven resilient and is going to get through this winter, but the level of damage to the economy, remains unclear. The Russian military is doing quite poorly this year in the war. For them, this is probably their worst year of combat performance since winter of twenty twenty-three. And it's clear that the way they've been fighting has reached diminishing returns, not in twenty twenty-six, but I would probably peg it as far back as summer of twenty twenty-five. They increasingly will face some manpower issues, and their effort now fixates more on strategic bombardment, which, while inflicting a lot of damage on Ukraine, has historically a challenge in that strategic bombardment does not have a great track record or even a good track record of achieving maximalist political aims in the war, especially if a ground campaign is unsuccessful or is floundering as Russia's is at this stage of the conflict. So the history of strategic bombardment as a way to try to win the war in the absence of the success of other efforts is not a good one. Although as an analyst, I'll tell you, most political leaders always think that it might work for them, even if you tell them that it doesn't. And so it's unsurprising to see that Russia's now leaning heavily towards strategic bombardment as a key pillar of its strategy. - I think it would also be nice to lay out the basics every time you bring them up. Maybe can you give a quick tangent of the twenty twenty-three offensive and then, what strategic bombardment is as opposed to the other mechanisms of war? - Sure. So in twenty twenty-three, there were a series of fairly set piece offensives and counter-offensives. After a partial mobilization with manpower replenished and some reserves established, Russia attempted a winter offensive, but its forces were unready. And so the winter campaign for Russia in twenty twenty-three was largely a failure, perhaps with the exception of the grinding battle over the city of Bakhmut. Then Ukraine launched a much-anticipated summer offensive using units that were freshly trained and equipped by Western countries. And there was a great deal of kind of hope and expectations that were placed upon this offensive, but it too failed. It lasted several months. I think in reality, it went from June twenty twenty-three till about November of twenty twenty-three. And then Russia tried to seize the initiative again and started its own offensive in fall twenty twenty-three with the Battle of Avdiivka. But so summer of twenty twenty-three is one of the periods where we still see, an exchange in terms of initiative between the two sides and fairly clear-cut major offensive operations and counter-offensive operations. And in twenty twenty-three early on, you have a failed Russian winter offensive. This is probably one of the worst points for the Russian military in the war, fall through winter, fall twenty twenty-two through winter of twenty twenty-three. And then you have the Ukrainian summer twenty twenty-three offensive, where Ukraine does gain some ground, but it's not what people hoped for. And since then, for much of the war, you know, you see Russia trying to establish and having an advantage in manpower and material. And for much of twenty-four and twenty- five, Russia actually tends to have the initiative, even though it's largely pursuing a grinding offensive on a very broad front. And if I sort of fast-forward and take us into twenty twenty-six, you really start to see the inflection point probably around fall of twenty twenty-five. And then in twenty twenty-six, the Russian effort is quite floundering, and Russian forces face significant reversals with the battle space a lot more dynamic this year. Ukraine has two of its own localized offensives running. and you see there's actually much greater fluidity in twenty twenty-six on the battlefield, certainly at the tactical level than you would in twenty-five or twenty-four. There's often a perception that it's just a positional stalemate. But in fact, even more recently, some of Ukraine's offensive operations had gained more terrain than Ukrainian forces were able to do during the summer twenty twenty-three offensive, which was planned to be a much bigger operation. - Also, it might be useful to kind of state perhaps the obvious, but the nature of this war -- one of the things, especially as it evolved, the role of drones on the front, and maybe this is where you can loop in strategic bombardment as well. Like, what are the main mechanisms of war here? - So we look at this war beyond what's happening at the front line. Russia has, from the very beginning of the war, had a series of strikes, an expansive strike campaign, but it really begins in fall 2022, where they begin launching combination strikes of long-range air-launched cruise missiles and short-range ballistic missiles against Ukrainian critical infrastructure. And by critical infrastructure, I mean power plants, substations, various types of heating plants, things that a country needs in order to sustain the economy and the population. And over time, those targets expand, right? Russia targets various types of civilian infrastructure. And actually, at this point in 2026, we've seen that campaign really broaden to include warehouses, data centers, schools, medical facilities, malls, actually quite a few shopping malls in the last few months, trains. So it's gone far beyond energy infrastructure to include a host of other civilian types of targets. And it changed over time from being primarily done with cruise missiles and ballistic missiles to being mostly conducted via saturation strikes using large numbers of one-way attack drones. And those drones themselves evolved in terms of the systems, gone now from being largely done with cheaper, easier to shoot down propeller-driven drones to ones that are jet-powered and are, in effect, light ground-launched cruise missiles, and a much larger number of ballistic missiles, some which are more sophisticated. And so Ukraine's been facing both large combination strikes, but also daily sustained pressure, constant attacks with jet-powered drones that generate alerts and that disrupt economic life and try to exhaust Ukraine's air defense. - By the way, I forgot to mention that I'm a big fan of both of yours. It's an honor, to have the both of you here, Mike and Preston. Preston, I've been watching you for a long time, so thank you for being here. So yes, to ask you, do you have, to build on what Mike was saying, and maybe can you also speak to some of the geographic areas that are in question here that are most contested? - Yeah, absolutely, Lex. Honor to be here. Always a challenge to add anything to what Mike has to say. We'll give it a shot here. I think it's good to get an idea of the areas that we're gonna be talking about. In Ukraine, the fight still is predominantly in the east and the southeast. So Kyiv, kind of in the middle of the country, is not facing direct Russian attacks in terms of infantry and short-range drones. They, of course, are on the receiving end daily of long-range drones and missile strikes. But as you move through the border region, starting in the north, there are Russian infiltrations in Sumy. There's also fighting in Ukrainian territory in Kharkiv. And then you get down into what's known as the Donbas, Luhansk, and Donetsk, and this is where some of the heaviest fighting throughout the war has taken place. And this is, I'm sure we'll get into it later, but an area referred to as the Fortress Belt that Ukraine has turned into just an absolutely brutal area for Russia to try to advance through. It is costing Russia a lot of people day in and day out. Moving from there, we're into Zaporizhzhia, and then Kherson butts up against the Black Sea. - And some of the strategic bombardment that Mike was talking about. So that's beyond the, even these areas. So even uh, Kyiv is being hit, so a lot of the places throughout Ukraine is being hit. - And some in the western portion of the country, not as frequently. Kyiv is a- ... a focus. - If you look along the front today, you have essentially some Russian border incursions trying to establish a small buffer across the border, which are lower intensity areas of fighting in Sumy, Kharkiv. You have an ongoing fighting around city of Kupyansk and Kharkiv region. And then you have the focus of Russian offensive efforts, Preston was saying, still trying to take the remainder of the Donbas, and that fighting ranges all the way down from cities like areas like Liman, all the way towards the main conglomeration of cities. And we should mention them now because I think they're gonna come up, that are remaining in the Donetsk region, which are Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, and Kostiantynivka, which troops all colloquially call Kostya, because its name's too long. And then further west of that is Dnipropetrovsk, which is a main city now that's been essentially an anchor in Ukrainian defense, west of that conglomeration, with another chain of cities behind it. And if we head southwest, we get into the Dnipro region and then Zaporizhzhia. And Zaporizhzhia is an interesting, fairly dynamic area because you have both Russian and Ukrainian forces on the offensive at the same time, where you have Russian forces trying to push west of, um, Huliaipole, and you have northeast of that, Ukrainian forces having had the initiative for much of the year. A tactical grouping of Ukraine air assault brigades has been running kind of a creeping offensive there, has been pretty successful in making gains. And the other area which we might get into later around Liman was Ukraine's Third Corps having conducted a successful offensive operation as well called Vihod. So those are two areas where Ukraine's not only contesting the initiative, but actually it's liberating territory, and in many ways wiping out Russian gains from 2025. And that's what I meant when I was saying earlier that this is a much more dynamic battle space than people think, in that territory is a lot more fluid. There's a vast gray zone, in fact, between the two lines. Ukraine does not hold cohesive defensive lines. It often has essentially pickets with small number of infantry that mark positions, but much of the territory is essentially contested such that in a battle space defined by dense control via drones and a sort of a sizable engagement zone, which varies from place to place, but you might say roughly it might be 15 kilometers forward and back of the front line. Although in some areas it's more, in other areas it's less. It depends. What happens is, in reality, that it becomes more of a gray zone, and as Preston was saying, Russian forces try to get past this drone engagement zone or defeat zone through infiltration. That's their main challenge, either through individual infantry, through light motorized attacks on motorcycles and ATVs, and they try to essentially get as far back past Ukrainian positions as they can, whereas Ukraine's largely defending with a combination of prepared defenses, minefields, and a large array of drones and drone units that are effectively engaging Russian forces before they get to their, even their own front line, their forward line of troops. And if they get past that point, they get past Ukrainian initial positions, then Ukrainian drone units essentially pick them up there. So it's, in many respects, kind of a zonal defense. But we should unpack that a bit because people see this as a drone war, and the statistics out there do show that drones inflict 80% of the losses. However, it is really a combination of things, and the dynamic is one that involves traditional defense and minefields that make it very hard for mechanized assaults or light motorized assaults to break through. Artillery, which still plays a role in the battlefield because it forces, the enemy forces to disperse, it has a shaping dynamic. Even if you don't use it much, the fact that it's present, it makes it hard for troops to concentrate or suppresses them. It slows them down in the assault, making them easy targets for drones. And it's still relevant because drones also have their own limitations, and two periods of the war when they often have limitations seasonally are spring and fall, again to the winter, because the weather becomes poor. You get high wind, you get rain. Drones don't work nearly as effectively during poor weather, and so artillery's a very important backup. And if you just had drones and you didn't have anything else, no minefields, no artillery, I don't think Ukraine would be able to hold the terrain this effectively with the low density of forces, the men that they currently have deployed. So it's important to describe as a combination of means, even if drones play such a central role, that folks don't ignore the interaction of these different capabilities in Ukraine's approach. - So sorry to linger on the basics, but, uh- ... can we, like, lay out, so artillery is big guns. What's the role of individual infantry? What's the role of tanks? What is this gray zone? What does it actually look like? How many drones are floating above? What does it look like, as Preston was saying, for an individual infantry soldier to, to run through that? Can you paint a picture of some of the basic things here? - Not good to run through that. It- ... it's terrifying. There's constant eyes in the sky, but to kind of walk this out a little bit, artillery generally speaking, 105 or 155 millimeter cannons. That's what we use here in the United States. It's primarily what Ukraine has been using now as it kind of shifted over to a NATO standard. You're talking about 20-ish kilometer range, which at a time was big, and there was a phase in this war where that was seemingly to determine the direction that it was gonna go. It was who had more artillery- ... who could mass fires in certain directions. It's just changed so drastically now to where the drone range has pushed those further and further back. So cannons are on the battlefield. There are some that are dug in, kind of in entrenched positions. Others are mobile on tracks or wheels 'cause they gotta get out of there. As soon as they fire, there's so many drones overhead watching them. When you get into the drones then on the battlefield, there's a number of them being utilized. Reconnaissance drones is kind of where everything starts, and those are just big fixed wing drones for the most part that they can stay airborne for quite a while. They're generally low cost, and that's been a dynamic that we've seen with both Russia and Ukraine in this war, is they've gone from the very few but high cost, maybe larger drones, down to a ton of low cost, borderline attritable. They don't wanna lose all these drones, but it's not that big of a deal to lose one compared to, say, a US Predator Reaper that costs, you know, 20-plus million dollars. So they've got these reconnaissance drones up constantly. Both sides have these up. When they spot something, that is passed along to the appropriate drone unit and it is engaged based off of their what they have available to them. The, I would say, most common one that we see, we see in terms of the media that has the most attention, would be the FPV drones. Those are small kind of quadcopters. You see them flying 12 inches, 18 inches. I think they might get up to 20 inches at times. Generally, there's a munition attached to the end of that. They crash it into something and it detonates. They can swap that out for anti-personnel munitions or go after vehicles or fortifications, and they can do that on the spot. So there are mountains of these FPVs. There was a picture of Kim Jong Un, actually, North Korea walking through a hallway of stacked FPVs. So these are the very small, low-cost, attritable drones, and they're being used. The numbers are staggering. - I'd say for FPVs, it's probably somewhere eight to 10,000 per day, just those, not including other types of tactical drones. And that would be for one side of the war. So to give you a sense that these are hundreds of thousands of these being employed per month. These strike capabilities exceed all the numbers of personnel and equipment on the battlefield by a very substantial amount. - And just to clarify, behind every FPV drone, there's a human being operating it. So there's also, from the news or something, there's a sense that autonomy is being utilized. It is not. So this is something you guys talked about. There's usually humans behind the drones. - Well, I'll be frank, most of this war are systems that are remotely operated, but they are operated by people. It is actually quite manpower- intensive. And in fact, it's, in many cases, if you look at both Russian and Ukrainian military, they had to build out substantial numbers of drone units and channel manpower into the drone component of the fight. It's not even a ratio of one to one, so one person to one drone. A typical drone team might require two or three people. You have a pilot, you have a co-pilot navigator. This is exhausting, tiring work. I'm not saying that other traditional missions are easy, but with a drone you have to be looking at a screen the whole time, all day. You have to be flying it, it's very intensive. Somebody else has to navigate. Another person might be the technician or the person who arms the system. And so almost all the systems in this war are remotely operated, whether they're flying drones, one-way attack strike drones, whether they're UGVs, uncrewed, you know, ground vehicles. And they require considerable support. At the end of the day, these are physical objects that require equipping, they require troubleshooting. And like most things in war, doesn't even - they don't even necessarily work well or right out of the box as well. It's what a lot of people don't necessarily appreciate about military affairs, that a lot of things don't necessarily work as intended on the battlefield. Somebody's gotta be there to fix it, they have to be there to check it. So the bottom line is that it is actually quite manpower intensive. There is a degree of semi-autonomy, terminal guidance and targeting at the very last point, or maybe the pilot can hit a box over a vehicle and then the drone knows that that's what it should go after, these kind of moments. And ways that the drone can overcome enemy electronic warfare or jamming with this kind of terminal guidance. But most of these use cases are a tiny percentage of the overall fight and the overall number of drones being employed in this war. I think in some ways, I hate to take away from the autonomy and artificial intelligence conversation. This war is testing that, and there are plenty of areas where I see it's being tested, but to some extent it's been over-hyped in terms of the percentages being, the percentage of the fight that's actually being run that way. It is very much, um, still a human-centric war with a lot of manpower involved running, operating, and maintaining all of these capabilities. - So one of the other novel aspects of this war is so much of it is televised, so that you could see videos from the drone perspective on both sides of that drone killing another human being. And one misconception I heard you talk about is that it takes one drone to accomplish that task, and it actually takes a lot more. Can you speak to that in terms of the number of drones it takes to accomplish a particular task, like to destroy a piece of technology or to I don't know the right way of speaking about this- - That's it. - But to kill another person. - Yeah. Eliminate a target might be a cold way of saying that. Um, we're in an interesting place where there's a lot of propaganda value in footage for anybody using it in any c- in any military right now in a way that we didn't have access to even just a few years ago. So there's a lot of interest in being able to show... I mean, we have seen now people will not take, reports that something happened unless there's a video of it. Which is insane because that, you know, a few years ago, you would never have expected to have video of a missile strike in Crimea on a Russian airfield. Now, if there's no video, it's maybe it didn't even happen. So the expectation is there and countries are meeting that by being able to say like, "Look, we penetrated your defenses. Look what we did," or, "Look at all the soldiers we killed as they were, we were making this approach." So it's out there. There's only a tiny fraction that's made public in the first place. And of those, that's only a tiny fraction of what actually accomplishes the mission. So drones, the batteries run out, they get jammed. All of a sudden the screen just goes dark. Sometimes they impact and they don't detonate. You know, all sorts of little things like that. That footage doesn't make it out. It in turn kind of creates this perception that one $300 drone or one $500 drone is eliminating a tank, and that's not happening. Maybe with the right munition and with a lucky shot and the tank isn't expecting it, maybe it's possible. Realistically, we're seeing 10, 20, I think upwards of 30 of these small drones at times being utilized to actually eliminate a tank. - So we should be imagining a very large number of FPV drones just hunting humans in tanks and technology. - The problem with understanding what the ratios are is the videos have a strong anchoring effect, and the videos are all videos of successes. There are no videos of misses. So unless you're actually there, you're able to collect the data, you don't know what percentage of hits or w- percentage of drones launched that really is. You might get easily the impression that 100% of the drones launch a hit. As Preston said, that's very far from the case. So you need quite a few drones. For people, even though on videos it looks like a one-to-one ratio, it's often not. I think it's often a lot closer to maybe five drones or something like that. - Per person? - Yeah, in practice. And I've seen, I'll be frank, I've myself seen videos that aren't public, where in the most extreme case, I saw one on a field trip in July where it took 12. On tanks, the most outside example I heard of a well-armored protected Russian tank with electronic warfare, one of these tanks that looks like a large barn, essentially, it's so, so heavily protected last year was 79. That's an extreme case, but most, as Preston said, is about 30 to 40. For an infantry fighting vehicle, about 15, maybe 15 to 20, depending, again. And you have some percentage of drones that are jammed, they don't make it to a target. You have some percentage of drones that may fail to detonate. So it's quite a few. And- You know, in talking to folks who are trying to return mobility and maneuver to the battlefield that specialize in drone-enabled mechanized assault, where they have both mechanized units and drone units supporting them, a company that, mechanized company that goes on the attack now expects to take about close to 300 hits in that assault. They expect vehicles to take quite a few hits, and most to be able to withstand them. So it does take quite a few drones, but the sheer saturation numbers of drones out there is very difficult to overstate. - So given that, what does a battle look like? How do you gain territory given these drone units, this huge amount of drones, this gray zone, also mentioning artillery, like you mentioned, and tanks? How do they work together in order to be able to do something like gain territory? - Well, they're doing it differently now. We're seeing a very different approach from Ukraine than we are from Russia. I can try to speak to the Russian part if you want to maybe take the Ukrainian offensive here in a second. But Russia has defaulted to more of a infiltration type tactic, where rather than large formations that get spotted, again, 10, 20, 30 kilometers away from the front, and they're then hunted down with long range drones. They don't even have the opportunity to get near the front line, so they stopped doing that. We started to see Russia move towards more motorized assaults with just pickup trucks, ATVs, even a lot of motorcycles at a point. Now it's mostly just individual infantrymen. They have checkpoints on a map. There's-- they're released, and they're sent forward five, 10, 20 kilometers trying to move to a forward location where they can consolidate. And again, the Ukrainian lines, they look clean on a map. They're not. There's a lot of gaps in there because a lot of it is being held with overhead drone coverage to just monitor approaches, and the Russians will get through. And one is a bit of a headache. Three becomes a bigger problem, and all of a sudden they're harassing supply lines, and that forces Ukrainian units to move back a little bit, forces Ukrainian drone pilots to move back a little bit, and that opens up the battlefield for more Russian soldiers to come forward just a little. There's a reason that the lines are moving so slowly right now. That infiltration is incredibly costly. We talked with an American volunteer, Marine, fighting with the First National Guard Corps as of in the Dobropillia direction a little over a year ago. He described this as an incredible tactic if you don't care about losing soldiers. He said, "It's great. You can just kind of chew through terrain. You can get there eventually. You're just gonna lose 90, 95% of your guys along the way." That's generally what we've seen from Russia over the course of the last at least six months, maybe a full year. Ukraine has been going about it in a different manner, especially with some of their recent counteroffensive stuff. - The way I look at it is first that in 2025, this war really began to be much more of a tug of war over who has superiority in this drone engagement zone, which forces locally call the kill zone. And the side that is able to suppress the other side's drone units through drone strikes, traditional artillery strikes, for Russia also heavy use of glide bombs, standoff glide bombs launched by Russian fixed wing aircraft, that side is then able to push the drone support further away from the front line, and then by displacing it, then be able to actually advance in that way. And so a lot of it's been a tug of war actually over who has superiority in drones and fire support. And increasingly on the Ukrainian side, where we see successful offensive operations, it's because you have, a very well thought through plan to set the conditions for the operation, begin to suppress Russian drone units, begin to interdict logistics behind the drone units so that they don't get sufficient supplies, begin to figure out how to potentially channel them by essentially pushing them into certain zones of operations where you can then localize, figure out where they're going to be when you're going to do the assault, then having a coordinated strike plan for how you're going to suppress them during the assault, and then now you've actually established the conditions for your forces to advance with some mobility and to dramatically reduce your losses. Because Ukraine cannot afford to fight the way Russia does. It doesn't have the manpower, and it doesn't... Even if it did have the manpower, it's not a question of numbers, it's a question of culture. Ukraine would not treat its forces in the same way. It wouldn't accept those kind of losses of its own troops. and so you've seen a couple different approaches on the Ukrainian side probably over the past year, and different assault units experimenting with them. You know, you have, uh, I think some advanced drone assault units like Code Nine Two and First Separate Assault Regiment that often work together, who are essentially using a combination of drones and very well-equipped and adapted mechanized formations to try to return maneuver to the battlefield and try to take terrain in a more mobile way, do it faster, rather than having a kind of slow-moving, grinding, creeping offensive. And you've seen all the way down to maybe the opposite side of the spectrum, air assault brigades very effectively employing three-man fire teams with drone support, systematically clearing tree line by tree line by tree line, slow and steady, but keeping their casualties low. This would be in the South and Zaporizhzhia. And on a broad front, still over time, over the course of this year, taking back a significant amount of terrain. And a bunch of other methods in between. So I won't say that there's been one method, but different units experimenting with different ways of doing it. And on the Russian side, as Preston said, It's a combination of mechanized light motorized assault sometimes, but increasingly Russians are using mechanized assault simply to consume the attention of Ukrainian drone units, to distract them or try to basically get them to focus on the mechanized assault so that light motorized assaults can get through, can get past their initial positions, all these soldiers on motorcycles and ATVs, and even believe it or not, I've seen Ladas and things of that nature. - For the infiltration side, like literally soldiers on motorcycles- ... trying to gain position- ... so they can then attack the supply chains to force Ukrainian forces to push back. - Let me maybe even take one minute just to explain why that's, that can be a challenge for Ukraine, 'cause it may sound to someone listening to this a bit preposterous, right? So let me offer why that can pose a challenge, and sometimes light motorized attacks have proven more successful than traditional mechanized attacks. Because mechanized attacks are a small number of vehicles. Typically, the leading vehicle has a big trawl to clear mines. You know, Ukrainian drones can easily gang up on it and then start isolating the column. And light motorized attacks is a whole number of soldiers. It could be 100 motorcycles, it could be more than 100 motorcycles, who are trying to use speed to overcome this sort of engagement zone. The reason why that can be an issue sometimes, even though most of them get taken out, I want to be clear, most of them are not successful. But Ukrainian forward positions are often three-man posts. They're not even really firing position observation posts. They're essentially pickets with considerable separation between them of several hundred meters, right? So Ukraine might have three of these for a kilometer. That means there's considerable space between them, so you could drive through. Then behind them, there might be secondary positions, but they're still pretty sparse in between. Most of the units involved in the fight are essentially supporting units, different type of fire support, drone support, traditional artillery fires, logistics, what have you. Many Ukrainian units don't really have the manpower to merely launch a counterattack if Russian forces break through. Some do, some have a quick reaction force ready, but for some, the manpower isn't necessarily there. So it can be a challenge if units do get through and they begin to accumulate. And what can happen, and this is how infiltration works for Russia, even though it's incredibly costly. You can imagine 10 soldiers going forward, and seven of them don't make it, but three do, and they found the path in between positions. So now the people that sent them know that this is the gap in Ukrainian positions, and they can then daisy chain send the next group down this path. Now, somewhere behind Ukrainian lines are now three Russian troops, but maybe it's five, six, seven. Now they're accumulating. Well, behind those positions, if you get three to five kilometers back, now you're reaching the first drone reconnaissance units that are flying Mavics. They are not prepared to receive an enemy assault team. They are flying drones, okay? So for them, this is already an issue because if Russian assault troops, if only three or four or five of them are operating your depth, and Ukrainian units do try to hunt them down, because if they let any number escape, then they get to the drone units, then you start losing your drone units, your support personnel. It is a real issue in the battle space. So that's essentially how infiltration works over time, although it's incredibly costly for Russia. It's a grim calculus. But it's a combination of that and also trying to fight for superiority in drone employment overall. Who has more drones? Who has more drone units in the fight? Who has more fire support? Who's able to suppress whose drone units to then allow their offensive tactics to have some purchase and success? - Quick pause. There's coffee downstairs for people just listening to this. This is late at night. We're pushing through. This is amazing. Okay, we're back. Uh, I guess I should also ask, what kind of drones are we talking about? So I just pulled out the, what is this? The Mini Pro- - It's a great one. - ... DJI drones. Uh, five. How many drones like this are there? And also, I should mention that some of them have a cable for them, right? Fiber optic cable. And I think Preston, you've talked about throughout all this. At first, you were skeptical when you visited initially, but then you kind of saw the, the wisdom, the effectiveness of the, of fiber optic drones. - The fiber optics are terrifying in a lot of ways. But to answer your question, the Mavics, those are still utilized. All things considered, they're relatively expensive compared to some other systems that Ukraine has. And those are not manufactured in Ukraine. And a lot of what they're using right now, they're building themselves. So FPVs are a bit bigger than that, but the term drone is so broad right now.
